newsitem.title: UK: Loyalists threaten staff in N.Irish prison row.
newsitem.headline: Loyalists threaten staff in N.Irish prison row.

text.p: Pro-British Loyalist militants warned on Tuesday they would retaliate if Northern Ireland prison authorities used force to break up a protest at a maximum security jail near Belfast.

The outlawed Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) issued the threat against prison officials and civil servants after convicted Protestant guerrillas tried to burn down two observation towers and staged rooftop protests at the Maze Prison to protest against new security measures.

The UFF, one of several Loyalist groups pledged to defend British rule against Irish Republican Army guerrillas, said in a statement telephoned to the BBC that "extreme conditions" had been forced on their associates in the prison, triggering daylong tension.

"Should the prison authorities give the go-ahead to the riot squads, on standby, to saturate the Loyalist wings and submit the men to unjust punishment, then we will be forced into a position whereby we will be obliged to ensure both the NIPS and NIO pay a price for the brutal treatment of our prisoners."

Managers of the Northern Ireland Prison Service (NIPS) ordered new cell searches and headcounts on Tuesday after an official of the Northern Ireland Office (NIO), the British department which runs the province, conducted an inquiry into a jail break attempt by IRA prisoners last month.
Trouble erupted during the morning when Loyalist prisoners refused to cooperate, saying they were being penalised for IRA wrong-doing.
Masked Loyalists clambered on to the roofs of two of the cellblocks at the Maze and waved Protestant emblems and makeshift banners.
They started fires at the base of metal watchtowers in two exercise yards, sending plumes of black smoke billowing above the heavily guarded complex.
Later British army vehicles patrolled the outside of the prison.
During previous periods of prison tension, Loyalist extremists have attacked prison officers at their homes.
Prison sources said staff were withdrawn from the cellblocks for their own protection and that family visits and other prisoner privileges had been suspended.
The search measures were aimed at tightening security in the wake of an attempted tunnel escape last month by IRA extremists serving terms for a waging war to end British rule.
The IRA plan was foiled when an officer discovered the tunnel. Prison sources said IRA prisoners had cooperated with the new security measures.
